signalBrief.text: This essay is a long, carefully staged argument about same-sex relationships inside Latter-day Saint belief, but it is also about a wider question: how a living church handles revelation, history, and human cost at the same time. The piece moves in layers. First it names the author’s position and stakes. Then it takes the strongest orthodox and affirming arguments seriously, especially through scripture and scholarship. Finally, it turns to Restoration history—plural marriage, race and priesthood, and the idea of continuing revelation—to ask what kinds of certainty the tradition can honestly sustain. The essay is not trying to flatten the conflict. It is trying to hold the conflict in view.

checkpoints.label: Where We Are
checkpoints.text: The opening has finished setting the emotional and rhetorical frame. The essay has not yet begun the argument itself; it has established that the writer is speaking from inside the tradition, with affection, grief, and caution. The crucible image at the end of this section is a way of saying that the essay will make room for conflict rather than rush to settle it.

checkpoints.label: Where We Are
checkpoints.text: We are now at the first major turn: the orthodox case has been set out as fully as possible, and the essay is ready to test it. The next movement does not dismiss tradition. It shifts into scripture scholarship, asking whether the biblical texts have been read with too much modern assumption and too little historical attention.

checkpoints.label: Where We Are
checkpoints.text: This midpoint closes the long textual section. The essay has argued that ancient prohibitions were aimed at forms of exploitation and domination, not contemporary same-sex marriage. But it also admits that this does not yet answer the Latter-day Saint question, because Restoration claims rest not only on ancient scripture but on modern revelation and prophetic authority.

checkpoints.label: Where We Are
checkpoints.text: The essay has now moved into Restoration history as a test case for whether doctrinal claims can change. Plural marriage and the priesthood restriction are not being used as side notes; they are the main precedent for asking whether a teaching framed as eternal can later be revised, disavowed, or re-understood.

checkpoints.label: Where We Are
checkpoints.text: The final movement is about what to do with unresolved tension. The essay does not claim that history and scripture have solved the issue. Instead, it argues that the Restoration itself trains believers to live with unfinished answers while still taking suffering, authority, and ongoing revelation seriously.

plainSignals.label: Plain Signal
plainSignals.text: This passage pauses to say, without softening, that the essay will not treat difficult church history as background noise. The mention of prison, exclusion, and disavowed teachings is doing structural work: it signals that the argument will not ask the reader to forget the parts of the past that remain spiritually and morally heavy.

plainSignals.label: Plain Signal
plainSignals.text: The fire image is important. It is not just decorative language about pain; it points toward a central claim that institutions, like people, can be both damaged and still worth staying in relation with. In plain terms, the essay is saying that brokenness does not automatically cancel meaning or covenant.

plainSignals.label: Plain Signal
plainSignals.text: The phrase “wild card” names the Restoration’s distinctive complication: Latter-day Saints cannot handle the question of sexuality only by arguing about ancient scripture, because they also believe in continuing revelation. That means both sides have to answer something harder than a simple proof-text debate.

plainSignals.label: Plain Signal
plainSignals.text: “Eternal increase” is being used here in a very specific theological way: not just continuation, but divine creation extending into eternity. The passage is pointing toward the LDS idea that exaltation is tied to a sealed, procreative male-female pair. This is one of the essay’s central pressure points.

plainSignals.label: Plain Signal
plainSignals.text: “Steadying the ark” is a warning story about overstepping divine order. Here it functions as a cultural and theological boundary marker: the essay is naming the LDS fear that sincere people may still be wrong if they place personal conviction above established authority.

plainSignals.label: Plain Signal
plainSignals.text: This paragraph is doing two things at once: it shows the writer as a ward teacher, and it gives a concrete example of how translation can change understanding. The point of hesed is not just that a Hebrew word is richer than English; it is that scholarship can expose a relationship-shaped meaning that gets flattened when language is smoothed over.

plainSignals.label: Plain Signal
plainSignals.text: Scroggs is being brought in to narrow the historical frame. The passage is pointing toward the possibility that Paul’s condemnations were aimed at exploitative practices common in the ancient world, not at the kind of mutual, adult same-sex partnership modern readers usually imagine.

plainSignals.label: Plain Signal
plainSignals.text: This is one of the essay’s sharpest moments. The point is not merely that a word changed in translation, but that a modern category was retrofitted onto older texts. In plain terms: the essay is challenging readers to notice how recent assumptions can quietly harden into doctrine-like certainty.

plainSignals.label: Plain Signal
plainSignals.text: The Utah landscape here is being used as evidence, not just scenery. Billboards, luxury, and temple-adjacent wealth are presented as a lived example of how selective moral concern works: some visible forms of status become normalized inside religious culture while other behaviors are singled out.

plainSignals.label: Plain Signal
plainSignals.text: This passage uses Matthew 19 to introduce a crucial idea: a command can be real and still fall short of the highest divine ideal. That matters because it creates room for the essay’s larger argument that prophetic law can be true for a time without being final.

plainSignals.label: Plain Signal
plainSignals.text: D&C 132 is being treated as a sign of the Restoration’s unfinished character. The essay is pointing out that Joseph Smith’s revelations did not just clarify existing teaching; they sometimes restructured the whole framework. That is why the author keeps returning to construction, expansion, and map-making imagery.

plainSignals.label: Plain Signal
plainSignals.text: McConkie’s statement is presented as a precedent for doctrinal humility. The key line is not just that leaders can be mistaken, but that they can speak from limited understanding and later need to yield to newer light. The essay treats this as a live LDS pattern, not a one-off apology.

plainSignals.label: Plain Signal
plainSignals.text: This passage gathers the essay’s major LDS concepts into one frame: accommodation, continuous revelation, the Ninth Article of Faith, and past reversals. The point is careful and narrow: none of these prove a change will happen, but they do make change thinkable inside the tradition.

plainSignals.label: Plain Signal
plainSignals.text: The closing image of the mapmaker and the territory is the essay’s final synthesis. It frames faith as movement under incomplete light: not certainty that the current route is perfect, but trust that the one who reveals can be followed while revelation continues.
